ordered_diagnoses: Cardiac Arrest due to Electrolyte Imbalance

facts.raw_span: A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest
the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier
then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom
He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes
Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation
A family member witnessed him struggling for air before losing consciousness
Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity
Sinus rhythm at approximately 100 beats per minute
Right axis deviation
Prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1
No acute occlusions found
QT interval of 360 ms measurable in leads V4-V6

concepts.why: The patient presented with cardiac arrest and pulseless electrical activity, which are common manifestations of acute coronary syndrome.
The patient had a history of COPD and was complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation, which suggests an exacerbation of COPD.
The patient's ECG showed a prolonged QT interval, which is a risk factor for cardiac arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.

concepts.preferred_label: Cardiac Arrest due to Electrolyte Imbalance
concepts.why: The patient's cardiac arrest may have been caused by an underlying electrolyte imbalance, which is suggested by the ECG findings of right axis deviation and prolonged QRS duration.
The patient's history of COPD and symptoms of shortness of breath and struggling for air suggest hypoxemic respiratory failure.
The patient's cardiac arrest and pulseless electrical activity are consistent with sudden cardiac death, which may have been caused by an underlying cardiac condition or electrolyte imbalance.

concepts.preferred_label: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) ruled out
concepts.why: The absence of acute occlusions found on coronary angiography explains the uncovered fact of no acute occlusions.
